title: FOMC Minutes — April 28–29, 2026
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2026-04-29 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

With Jerome Powell chairing (Kevin Warsh chaired the next meeting, in June), the Committee held the federal funds range at 3.50–3.75%. IORB stayed at 3.65% and the primary credit rate at 3.75%. The statement said: "Inflation is elevated, in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices." The vote was 8–4, with dissents coming from both directions. Stephen Miran wanted a 25bp cut. Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan agreed with holding but objected to keeping the statement's easing bias. They wanted a more two-sided description of future rate moves.

Economic outlook

Staff saw activity slightly stronger than in March, with GDP growing a bit faster than potential. Unemployment was expected to stay near its longer-run rate and then edge slightly below it in 2028. Staff saw risks to growth and employment tilted to the downside.

Inflation

Inflation moved higher. Headline PCE was 2.8% in February and core was 3.0%. Staff estimated March at 3.5% headline and 3.2% core. Participants pointed to energy, tariffs, shipping and fertilizer costs. Several also noted that rising software prices were lifting core inflation. Staff expected higher inflation this year, then easing toward 2% by the end of next year, with risks skewed to the upside. Near-term expectations rose, while longer-term expectations were seen as stable.

Labor market

Unemployment was 4.3% in March. Job gains were low on average, but conditions had stabilized. Most participants still saw downside risks to employment, citing firms delaying hiring because of uncertainty and AI adoption.

Financial markets & balance sheet

Stocks rose and corporate bond spreads narrowed over the period. Markets priced little change in rates this year, with options implying about a 30% chance of a hike by Q1 2027. Private credit saw redemptions but showed some signs of stabilizing. Staff rated vulnerabilities as notable, citing elevated asset valuations, high hedge fund leverage in Treasuries and private credit. The Desk continued buying bills to keep reserves ample. Swap lines with five central banks and with Canada and Mexico were renewed unanimously. Securities lending began on FedTrade Plus on April 22. There was no FX intervention.

Risks participants flagged

  • A prolonged Middle East conflict or persistently high oil prices lifting inflation and loosening the anchor on expectations
  • Higher tariffs
  • A sharp drop in labor demand
  • Private credit losses spreading to wider credit markets, or hedge funds unwinding Treasury positions
  • AI-related cybersecurity threats

What it signaled about next moves

This was a hawkish turn. Almost all participants backed holding, and the Committee was still described as well positioned to respond to incoming data. Several said cuts would make sense once disinflation was firmly on track or the labor market clearly weakened. But a majority said firming could become appropriate if inflation kept running persistently above 2%, and many would have dropped the easing-bias language. As before, "monetary policy was not on a preset course."

Read-through for SPY

  • A majority openly discussing possible hikes, plus four dissents, showed the Fed's bias moving from cuts toward tightening. That pressures equity multiples.
  • Stocks still rose and credit spreads narrowed over the period, so the market was looking past rates for now. Even so, the Fed flagged elevated valuations.
  • A jump in headline inflation driven by energy is the key variable to watch. Oil prices became a direct driver of the rate outlook.
